final_proof:
Let $f$ be the continuous $2\pi$-periodic function whose restriction to $[-\pi,\pi]$ is $f(x)=x^2$. The periodic extension is continuous because the two endpoint values are both $\pi^2$.

We first justify the Fourier convergence fact that we will use. If $h$ is any continuous $2\pi$-periodic function, its $N$-th Fejér mean is
$$\sigma_Nh(x)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^N\left(1-\frac{n}{N+1}\right)(a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx),$$
where $a_n,b_n$ are its Fourier coefficients. The finite geometric-sum identity gives
$$\sigma_Nh(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}h(x-t)K_N(t)\,dt,\qquad K_N(t)=\frac1{N+1}\left(\frac{\sin((N+1)t/2)}{\sin(t/2)}\right)^2,$$
with the value at $t=0$ understood by continuity. Indeed, expanding the square of $\sum_{j=0}^N e^{ijt}$ gives the stated Fourier weights. In particular, $K_N\geq0$ and
$$\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}K_N(t)\,dt=1.$$

These formulas prove that $\sigma_Nh\to h$ uniformly. Given $\varepsilon>0$, uniform continuity of $h$ supplies $0<\delta<\pi$ such that $|h(x-t)-h(x)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|t|<\delta$, uniformly in $x$. If $M=\max|h|$, then
$$|\sigma_Nh(x)-h(x)|\leq\varepsilon+\frac{2M}{2\pi}\int_{\delta\leq|t|\leq\pi}K_N(t)\,dt.$$
On the latter set,
$$K_N(t)\leq\frac1{(N+1)\sin^2(\delta/2)},$$
so the second term tends to zero uniformly in $x$. Thus $\sigma_Nh\to h$ uniformly.

We now compute the Fourier coefficients of $f$. Since $f$ is even, all sine coefficients vanish. Also,
$$a_0=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2\,dx=\frac{2\pi^2}{3}.$$
For $n\geq1$, two integrations by parts give
$$\begin{aligned}a_n&=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos(nx)\,dx\\&=\frac2\pi\left[\frac{x^2\sin(nx)}n+\frac{2x\cos(nx)}{n^2}-\frac{2\sin(nx)}{n^3}\right]_0^\pi=\frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}.\end{aligned}$$
Consequently the formal Fourier series is
$$S(x)=\frac{\pi^2}{3}+4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n\cos(nx)}{n^2}.$$
It converges absolutely and uniformly, by comparison with $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^{-2}$, which converges by the integral test. Its Fejér means converge uniformly to $S$: split the absolutely convergent series into a finite initial segment, on which the weights $1-n/(N+1)$ tend to $1$, and a uniformly small absolute tail. But the Fejér theorem just proved says that these same means converge uniformly to $f$. Hence $S(x)=f(x)$ for every $x$.

Taking $x=\pi$ and using $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n$ yields
$$\pi^2=\frac{\pi^2}{3}+4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}.$$
Therefore
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{n^2}=\frac14\left(\pi^2-\frac{\pi^2}{3}\right)=\frac{\pi^2}{6}.$$
By the definition of the Riemann zeta function for real part greater than one, the series on the left is $\zeta(2)$. Thus $\boxed{\zeta(2)=\pi^2/6}$.
